text: A feature is an input the model uses. We keep six numeric readings and one category, product type. Air and process temperatures use kelvin. Torque describes twisting force. Tool wear is measured in minutes. Vibration RMS summarizes vibration strength and is simulated here. Leave out the answer and anything recorded after a failure. IDs and unused extra fields stay out too. Ask: would we know this value when making a prediction? We have few inputs, so there is no need to compress them using PCA. Sources: src/reference.ipynb section 5; artifacts/machine_failure_metadata.json.

If training results are much better, the model may be memorizing details that do not carry over. The deep tree in the notebook demonstrates this. Source: src/reference.ipynb section 7.

title: How well did the model do?

text: How well did the model do?
textPreview: How well did the model do?

text: 88.2% recall
60 of 68 failures detected
31.6% precision
60 of 190 alerts were failures
8 missed failures     130 false alarms

Accuracy 93.1%     F1 0.465
Average precision 0.688     ROC-AUC 0.974
A high accuracy score can still hide missed failures
textPreview: A high accuracy score can still hide missed failures

text: Recall asks: how many real failures did we catch? We caught 60 out of 68, or 88.2%. Precision asks: how many alerts were correct? 60 out of 190, or 31.6%. We missed 8 failures and raised 130 false alarms. Accuracy is the share of all predictions that were correct. F1 combines precision and recall in one score. Average precision and ROC-AUC summarize how well scores separate failures from normal rows across different cutoffs. Average precision is not the same calculation as area under the precision-recall curve. These are the saved test results. Always saying normal would give 96.6% accuracy but catch no failures. Sources: artifacts/machine_failure_metadata.json; local/STREAMING.md.

textPreview: See the model score, prediction, known answer and results so far | The model sees the readings. We use the known answer to check it.

text: Switch to the terminals. Start Kafka and create the topic using local/STREAMING.md if needed. Use the Python environment that matches the saved model. The producer sends test rows. Kafka carries them. The consumer runs the saved model and prints the result. The model uses only machine readings. The known answer is included separately so the demo can check predictions. Repeating these rows does not give new evidence about model quality. Missing sensor values are filled and flagged. Invalid values are skipped. Real machines usually need a later confirmed outcome before we can check a prediction. Sources: src/producer.py; src/consumer.py; local/STREAMING.md.

text: This is a proposed application. The user supplies a question and machine readings. The AI assistant knows the prediction tool and the inputs it needs. It chooses that tool. The app checks the inputs and runs the saved model with its settings. The tool returns the score, prediction, cutoff and any warnings. The assistant uses that result to explain the answer. The app also includes the original tool output unchanged. The assistant must not invent readings or change the prediction. If the input or tool fails, ask for details or show an error. DAG means directed acyclic graph: the steps and arrows show one request moving forward without a loop. Kafka is used in the earlier demo; this direct tool call does not need Kafka.
